title: Huckleberry Finn
objective: After this level you can explain why Twain's novel told in a boy's own voice changed American writing and still sparks debate.
summary: Twain let Huck narrate a whole novel in his own speech, a break writers such as Hemingway saw as the start of modern American writing. Huck's choice to help Jim anchors a still-live debate.

cards.headline: This novel opens by threatening to shoot anyone who looks for a plot.
cards.body: Before the story of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn begins, Mark Twain posts a notice: "persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot." It's a joke, and a warning: this book won't sound like a lesson.

cards.headline: A boy tells it his way
cards.body: Then Huck starts talking: "You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter." The whole novel stays in his voice. Critic Tony Tanner called that revolutionary: earlier books let rough-spoken characters talk, but always inside a polished adult narrator's frame. Here the boy owns the book. Ernest Hemingway later declared that all modern American literature comes from it.

cards.headline: The wrong reason to do the right thing
cards.body: Huck, a poor white boy, befriends Jim, a man who has escaped slavery. Huck has been taught that helping Jim is a sin. He writes a letter that would betray Jim, then tears it up: "All right, then, I'll go to hell." He believes he is damning himself by doing right. Defenders read the book as satire, and this is their evidence: the joke is on a society whose idea of sin is upside down.

cards.headline: Still argued over
cards.body: The arguments began early: soon after publication, the book was banned in Concord, Massachusetts. Today they turn on race. Critics point to its repeated racial slur and a portrayal of Jim along minstrel-show lines; in 2000 the Pennsylvania NAACP and professor Jonathan Arac wanted it off required reading lists. Defenders such as scholar Jocelyn Chadwick argue for teaching it as satire of racism. Satire or Evasion? (1992), essays by African American scholars, spans the whole range.

questions.prompt: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is narrated by _____.

options.label: Twain, as a polished adult
options.rationale: Twain hands the whole book to Huck.

options.label: Jim, looking back years later
options.rationale: Jim is a character, not the narrator.

options.label: Tom Sawyer
options.rationale: Tom had his own earlier book.

options.label: Huck himself, in his own voice

questions.explanation: Huck narrates from the first line, and the whole novel stays in his vernacular voice.

questions.prompt: Match each person with what they said or wanted.
questions.explanation: Jocelyn Chadwick argues for teaching the book as satire of racism, Jonathan Arac wanted it off required reading lists, and Ernest Hemingway said all modern American literature comes from it.

questions.prompt: Level 2's fables usually state their moral at the end. What does Twain's opening notice threaten anyone who looks for a moral?

options.label: Being shot
options.rationale: That's the penalty for looking for a plot.

questions.explanation: Twain jokes that "persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished", the reverse of a fable's stated moral.
